excerpt: You can change personal injury lawyers at almost any stage in Georgia or South Carolina. How the switch works, and what it costs you.
keyTakeaways: You have the legal right to switch personal injury lawyers at any time in both Georgia and South Carolina under Rule 1.16 of each state's Rules of Professional Conduct. Warning signs include unreturned calls, no case updates, pressure to settle low, and inexperience with your case type. Your first attorney may claim a fee for work already done — in Georgia secured by a lien on the case under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14; South Carolina has no attorney's-lien statute and measures the claim by the reasonable value of the work (Rule 1.5(a), Rule 407 SCACR). Switching is easiest during pre-litigation and becomes harder near trial. Georgia's 2-year (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) statutes of limitations make prompt action critical.

faqs.question: Can I fire my personal injury lawyer in the middle of my case?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to terminate your attorney at any time and for any reason. This right is protected under each state's Rules of Professional Conduct (Rule 1.16). Your lawyer cannot hold your case hostage, and they must return your file and cooperate with the transition to your new attorney.

faqs.question: Will I owe my first lawyer money if I switch?
faqs.answer: Possibly. A lawyer you discharge before your case resolves cannot collect the contract percentage, but may claim the reasonable value of the work already done. In Georgia that claim is secured by a lien on the case under O.C.G.A. § 15-19-14 and measured in quantum meruit (Ellerin & Assocs. v. Brawley, 2003). South Carolina has no attorney's-lien statute; the claim is measured by the reasonableness factors in Rule 1.5(a) of the Rules of Professional Conduct, and a lien on your recovery exists only if your fee agreement creates one (Eleazer v. Hardaway Concrete Co., 1984). Your new attorney can negotiate or dispute any unreasonable claim.

faqs.question: When is it too late to switch personal injury lawyers?
faqs.answer: While you always have the right to fire your attorney, switching becomes more difficult once a case is close to trial. A judge may deny a continuance request if changing lawyers would significantly delay proceedings. Switching is easiest during the investigation, treatment, or pre-litigation negotiation phases.

faqs.question: What are the warning signs I should switch lawyers?
faqs.answer: Common red flags include unreturned phone calls or emails for weeks at a time, no case updates, pressure to accept a low settlement, lack of experience with your case type, your case being handed off to junior associates without notice, and missed deadlines or filing errors. Trust your instincts — if you feel your case is not being prioritized, it may be time for a change.

faqs.question: How do I transfer my case to a new lawyer?
faqs.answer: First, consult with a new attorney to confirm they will take your case. Then send written notice to your current attorney terminating the relationship. Request your complete case file in writing. Your former attorney must comply and transfer your file. If a lawsuit is already pending, the change of counsel also goes through the court (Uniform Superior Court Rule 4.3 in Georgia; Rule 11(b), SCRCP in South Carolina). Your new lawyer will handle the transition, review the file, and continue your case from where it left off.

faqs.question: Will switching lawyers hurt my case?
faqs.answer: Not if done properly and promptly. A responsive, experienced attorney can improve your outcome compared with staying with one who is neglecting your case. The key is to switch early enough that your new lawyer has time to build the strongest possible case before any deadlines or trial dates.
